record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.original_question: What primordial materials were Titan, its crust, its interior, and its nitrogen-methane atmosphere built from, and can measurements such as Titan's moment of inertia, stable-isotope ratios, noble-gas abundances, crustal deuterium-to-hydrogen in water, gravity-field harmonics, and tidal Love numbers distinguish among possible building-block compositions and atmospheric-origin scenarios?

evidence.quote: 1) What were the building blocks of Titan?

Our current sparse constraints regarding Titan’s interior permit multiple interpretations of its core composition. The moment of inertia (C/MR2 ∼0.34) from gravity measurements by Cassini (Iess et al., 2010; Iess et al., 2012; Durante et al., 2019) can be modeled in several ways, including a bimodal model with a mixture of low density and high-density components (Néri et al., 2020), or a more uniform composition lacking in significant amounts of iron (Vance et al., 2018).

Other atmospheric quantities can in principle provide constraint on building blocks, such as the ratios of stable isotopes (D/H, 12C/13C, 14N/15N, 16O/18O, etc) (Pinto et al., 1986; Wong et al., 2002; Jennings et al., 2008; Mandt et al., 2009; Nixon et al., 2012; Mandt et al., 2012), stable noble gas abundances (20Ne and 22Ne, 36Ar and 38Ar) and the abundances of radiolytic elements (e.g. 40Ar) (Glein, 2015; Miller et al., 2019), as described in Chapter 3.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider Saturn's moon Titan, a body of mass M and radius R possessing a substantial nitrogen–methane atmosphere, an icy crust, and a partially differentiated interior. Available observational constraints include: (i) the normalized polar moment of inertia C/(MR^2) ≈ 0.34 inferred from gravitational measurements; (ii) atmospheric stable-isotope ratios D/H, 12C/13C, 14N/15N, and 16O/18O; (iii) noble-gas abundances, in particular 20Ne, 22Ne, 36Ar, 38Ar, and the radiogenic 40Ar; (iv) the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio of water in the crust; (v) low-degree gravity-field harmonics (e.g. J2, C22); and (vi) tidal Love numbers (e.g. k2, h2).

Problem. Identify the primordial materials from which Titan as a whole, its icy crust, its rocky/metallic interior, and its nitrogen–methane atmosphere were assembled. In particular:

(a) Determine whether the observed moment of inertia C/(MR^2) ≈ 0.34 is uniquely explained by a bimodal interior model containing a mixture of low-density (hydrated silicate/ice) and high-density (anhydrous silicate plus iron) components, or alternatively by a more uniform interior composition essentially lacking metallic iron, or by some other admissible composition.

(b) Determine whether the listed stable-isotope ratios, noble-gas abundances, radiogenic 40Ar abundance, crustal water D/H ratio, gravity-field harmonics, and tidal Love numbers can collectively discriminate among candidate building-block compositions (e.g. comet-like volatile-rich planetesimals vs. drier inner-Saturnian-system material) and among competing atmospheric-origin scenarios (primordial capture, delivery via accreted ices, outgassing from the interior, or photochemical/late-stage processing).

State which combinations of these measurements suffice to uniquely constrain the building blocks, or prove that no such unique determination is possible from the listed observables alone.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an explicitly posed open question in Titan science. Current observational constraints admit multiple interior and atmospheric-origin models, and resolution is expected to require future missions (e.g., Dragonfly) and additional measurements. No published work uniquely identifies Titan's building blocks.

status_evidence.snippet: Chapter outlining unresolved questions about Titan, including the building blocks of Titan and its atmosphere.
status_evidence.claim: The question of Titan's building blocks is presented as an open research direction requiring future measurements.
